# Exploration of auditory statistical learning, socioeconomic status, and language outcomes in Bangladeshi children: An fNIRS study

**Authors:** Eileen F. Sullivan; Laura Pirazzoli; John E. Richards; Talat Shama; Alexandre Chaumette; Rashidul Haque; William A. Petri; Charles A. Nelson

**Affiliations:** aBoston Children’s Hospital, Boston MA, USA | bHarvard Graduate School of Education, Cambridge, MA, USA | cHarvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | dUniversity of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA | eInternational Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Dhaka, Bangladesh | fHarvard College, Cambridge, MA, USA | gUniversity of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA, USA

## Abstract

Auditory statistical learning, or the ability to detect statistical regularities in continuously presented stimuli, is thought to be one element that underlies language acquisition. Prior studies have uncovered behavioral and neural correlates of statistical learning, yet additional work is needed from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) to explore whether statistical learning varies across cultures or underlies associations often found between socioeconomic status (SES) and language outcomes. In the current study, we explored the feasibility of using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to explore auditory statistical learning in Bangladesh, a lower-middle income country. Participants were 102 two-year-old (M = 25.72 months, SD = 2.07 months) and 125 five-year-old children (M = 62.35 months, SD = 2.46 months) living in a low-income urban neighborhood of Dhaka (average family income of 28,145.13 Bangladeshi Takas or 260.06 USD per month). We also collected measures of SES and language outcomes. Brain responses during the statistical learning paradigm could be detected with fNIRS in both two- and five-year-olds, with two-year-olds exhibiting a higher response to predictable sequences and five-year-olds exhibiting higher responses to unpredictable sequences. fNIRS correlates of statistical learning were not related to language outcomes but were associated with SES in the five-year-old cohort. This study demonstrates the utility of employing fNIRS to study the neural correlates of statistical learning in LMICs and the feasibility of expanding the representativeness of the existing literature. These findings also highlight potential areas for inquiry into how SES may relate to individual differences in statistical learning responses.

Language skills serve as essential building blocks for a wide range of outcomes throughout the life course such as social communication abilities, academic performance, and job success (Demir & Küntay, 2014). Statistical learning, defined as the ability to discover patterns in continuous stimuli, is one early foundational process thought to underlie appropriate language acquisition and development (Romberg & Saffran, 2010). The implicit tracking of the probabilities in auditory patterns, or auditory statistical learning, has been linked to the proper categorization of speech sounds, word-segmentation, and rule-learning, which together facilitate language acquisition (Wu & Bulut, 2020). Complementing and supplementing behavioral studies of statistical learning, recent work has begun to establish neural processes underlying auditory statistical learning, deepening our understanding of the mechanistic foundations of language acquisition (Roberts & Kaiser, 2011; Stanton-Chapman et al., 2002).

Prior neuroimaging studies, mostly conducted with adult participants, have implicated multiple brain regions in auditory statistical learning. The superior temporal gyrus (STG), a region involved broadly in auditory processing, is frequently activated during tasks involving the detection of structured streams of speech in adults and infants (Schiavo & Froemke, 2019, Tremblay et al., 2013; Arimitsu et al., 2011; Emberson et al., 2015). Additionally, the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), including Broca’s area, is thought to be involved in domain-general uncertainty processing and prediction and has been implicated in statistical learning in adults and infants (Fedorenko et al., 2012; Karuza et al., 2013; Abla & Okanoya, 2008; Arimitsu et al., 2011). Yet, while the IFG and STG have been implicated in auditory statistical learning in both infancy and adulthood, few neuroimaging studies have assessed statistical learning during the toddler and early-childhood periods.

It is important to examine statistical learning across development, as differences in responses to unpredictable (novel) versus predictable (familiar) sequences have been found across study populations, sparking debate on the trajectories and origins of these differences. Infant studies of sensitivity to auditory patterns using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) have shown higher brain activity during novel sequences than during familiar sequences (Arimitsu et al., 2011; Emberson et al., 2015). In contrast, neuroimaging studies with adults have often found higher brain activity during more familiar sequences than novel sequences (Abla & Okanoya, 2008; Hasson & Tremblay 2016). Responses to novel and familiar stimuli can depend on modality, stimuli type, training length, individual differences, and a range of other factors (Isbilen & Christiansen, 2022). Given the paucity of neuroimaging studies across the toddler and early-childhood periods, it is unclear whether we should expect more infant-like or adult-like patterns of responses to familiar versus novel auditory sequences in relevant brain regions. Notably, both larger or smaller brain responses to familiar versus novel auditory sequences would indicate statistical learning abilities, as either would demonstrate the ability to extract and differentiate auditory sequences based on their level of predictability.

An additional gap in the literature stems from the fact that much of the existing literature on statistical learning has been conducted in high-income countries (HICs), and thus current findings are not representative of children globally. While statistical learning has widely been thought of as a universal and domain-general process, this assumption remains untested without additional studies from a wider range of contexts to assess whether statistical learning may instead be context-dependent (Nielsen et al., 2017). In recent decades, neuroimaging techniques have been increasingly deployed in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), affording the opportunity to probe cognitive processes such as statistical learning in a more diverse range of contexts (Jensen et al., 2019; Lloyd-Fox et al., 2019). With these advances in the accessibility of neuroimaging technology, it is now possible to investigate the neural correlates of statistical learning in more diverse contexts to investigate potential cross-cultural variations or similarities.

In addition to the need to understand whether the neural bases of statistical learning are universal or may vary between contexts, it is essential to probe individual differences in the neural correlates of statistical learning within a given context. Associations between socioeconomic status (SES) and language outcomes have been well-established in the literature, with children growing up in more disadvantaged circumstances more likely to have lower scores on language assessments (Perkins et al., 2013; Hackman et al., 2010). Yet, it is unknown whether the neural correlates of statistical learning could partially explain these associations found between SES and behavioral language outcomes. While behavioral studies have repeatedly shown that statistical learning abilities are associated with language skills such as productive vocabulary, syntactic understanding, and reading (Kidd & Arciuli, 2016; Evans, 2009), neuroimaging studies are needed to investigate the neural mechanisms that may underlie these behavioral associations. Furthermore, recent work has begun to suggest that neural responses during statistical learning may be linked to early experiences (Pierce et al., 2021; Wang & Saffran, 2014), yet additional work (especially in LMICs) is needed to more comprehensively investigate how variation in measures of SES may relate to statistical learning. Identifying whether individual differences in the neural correlates of statistical learning can help to explain associations between SES and language outcomes could aid in the earlier identification of children at risk of language deficit and could inform early intervention strategies within a given context.

Statistical learning could vary across or within contexts via various mechanistic pathways. For instance, experiences commonly present in certain contexts but not others, such as malnutrition, could lead to differences in the activation of temporal and frontal brain regions (Jensen et al., 2021; Turesky et al., 2021). Given that statistical learning has been shown to rely on the IFG and STG, it is plausible that early alterations in brain architecture in frontal and temporal regions could have downstream consequences on statistical learning abilities. Additionally, children growing up in low SES families or contexts are more likely to experience lower quantity or quality of language exposure (Perkins et al., 2013). Children who have fewer opportunities to “practice” extracting statistical probabilities in auditory patterns in their natural environments due to lower language exposure could have delayed trajectories of statistical learning abilities. SES has also been shown to be related to lower gray and white matter, as well as altered functional connectivity, which could impact the efficiency of neural circuits underlying auditory processing (Turesky et al., 2021).

To begin to explore and tease apart these potential sources of between- and within-context variation in statistical learning, additional studies in LMICs are needed to expand the diversity of populations represented in the literature and offer opportunities to investigate the statistical learning abilities of children growing up in very low SES families and contexts. In the present study, we seek to explore the feasibility of examining neural signatures of statistical learning abilities in an LMIC context using fNIRS. fNIRS is an optimal tool to chart brain development in historically under-represented samples such as LMIC populations, as it is relatively low-cost, motion-tolerant, portable, and easy to implement in studies of infants and children (Blasi et al., 2019). fNIRS has been successfully deployed in developmental studies in LMICs, with studies deploying paradigms that require little adaptation across contexts to probe different aspects of neurodevelopment in understudied populations (Lloyd-Fox et al., 2019; Blasi et al., 2019; Pirazzoli et al., 2022). Yet, fNIRS has not yet been utilized to examine statistical learning in toddlers and young children in LMICs. fNIRS can open the door to expanding the diversity of populations represented in the literature to understand the extent to which statistical learning is universal or context- or experience-dependent. Thus, in this study we capitalize on the advantages of fNIRS to conduct the first investigation of the neural signatures of statistical learning in two- and five-year-olds in an LMIC, utilizing a non-linguistic paradigm that could be easily deployed in diverse contexts with minimal need for adaptation. The data used in this paper are drawn from the wider Bangladesh Early Adversity Neuroimaging (BEAN) study, which focuses on investigating relations among environmental factors, brain development, and cognition in children living in Dhaka, Bangladesh, an urban area of concentrated poverty (Jensen et al., 2021; Pirazzoli et al., 2022). The current analyses focus on exploring auditory statistical learning in this population by utilizing fNIRS data, and examining how these fNIRS correlates relate to children’s SES and language abilities in two cross-sectional cohorts of children (two- and five-year-olds).

We sought to address two main aims in the current study. Our first aim was to explore the feasibility of assessing correlates of auditory statistical learning in two- and five-year-old Bangladeshi children using fNIRS and a tone-based paradigm. Our goal was to demonstrate the utility of deploying neuroimaging in LMICs to assess statistical learning and potentially identify a non-linguistic paradigm that could be easily deployed in LMIC in diverse settings without extensive adaptation to index statistical learning. To assess the feasibility of this methodology in this setting, we investigated how children discriminated auditory patterns of varying levels of predictability at these ages and which brain regions were implicated in differentiating these patterns. We hypothesized that both age cohorts would exhibit the largest difference in hemodynamic responses between the highly familiar and novel conditions. Given the literature presented above and the lack of statistical learning studies in these age groups, we did not have a priori hypotheses about whether children will have higher activation during novel versus familiar tone sequences. Our second aim was to explore whether fNIRS responses during the statistical learning paradigm were sensitive to within-context variation in children’s SES or language abilities. Our goal was to understand whether this paradigm could be used as an index of individual differences within a particular LMIC context. We predicted that children with lower SES would show smaller differences in their responses to the highly familiar and novel conditions. We also expected that children who exhibited larger differences between the highly familiar and novel conditions would tend to have higher scores on language assessments, as discrimination of auditory patterns may support the development of language skills.

## Methods

### Participants

Participants were drawn from two separate cohorts of children living in the Mirpur neighborhood of Dhaka and taking part in the BEAN study. fNIRS data included in the current analyses were collected from 102 two-year-olds (M = 25.72 months, SD = 2.07 months; 56 females, 50 males) and 125 five-year-olds (M = 62.35 months, SD = 2.46 months; 42 females, 83 males). On the day of fNIRS data collection, behavioral assessments of cognitive development were also performed. Measures of SES were collected from primary caregivers at six months for the younger cohort and at three years old for the older cohort. All data were collected by fully trained local staff in a medical clinic in Mirpur. Children were excluded from the study if they were born less than 33 weeks gestational age, had a history of brain injury, neurological abnormalities, genetic disorders, or visual or auditory impairments. The original sample included 210 participants from each age group. (Data attrition information below.) Ethical approval of this study was obtained from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at Boston Children’s Hospital and the research and ethics committee at the International Centre for Diarrheal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b).

### Stimuli

Children listened to a passive auditory statistical learning task either at two or five years old (Figure 1). The script to present the paradigm is available at https://github.com/eilysullivan/fNIRS_statlearning. The task began with a four-minute training phase that consisted of a continuous stream of “tone-words”, each made up of three pure tones, presented in a random order. There were 248 tone-words presented during the training phase. Next, a four-minute test phase was presented, where blocks of three conditions were presented with a baseline block of silence between experimental blocks. The three conditions differed in their transition probability (TP), defined as the likelihood that tones appear next to each other in an auditory sequence (Soares et al., 2020). Each block was 10 seconds long and consisted of one tone-word repeated eight times. The three conditions were: High TP, Low TP, and Novel. In the High TP (100% probability) condition, the tone word in the test phase perfectly matched a tone word repeatedly presented in the training phase and was therefore highly predictable. In the Low TP (50% probability) condition, the tone word in the test phase was also presented in the training phase repeatedly. In half of the presentations in the training phase, the tone word appeared in the same exact order as in the test phase, whereas in the other half of presentations in the training phase, the two last tones in the tone word were flipped. Thus, this condition was somewhat predictable. In the Novel TP (0% probability) condition, the tone word in the test phase had not previously appeared during the training phase and therefore was not predictable. The same tone word was used in each of the blocks of a certain condition in the test phase. The baseline trials were silent and lasted 9–13 seconds (randomly jittered). A maximum of 12 experimental trails were presented (four trials per condition). There were four different orders of experimental blocks, randomized across participants. Run types included: A – NHNLNHNHLNLH, B – HNLNHLHLNHLN, C – LHNLNHNHLNLH, D – LHNLNHNHLNLH (H=High TP, L=Low TP, N=Novel). fNIRS responses of children exposed to the different run types were compared by performing a repeated-measures ANOVA for each condition contrast with run type included as a between-subjects factor and no main effect of run type was found (p-values > .734). Children watched a silent cartoon with animals during the presentation of the task to increase compliance and reduce motion during the task.

### fNIRS Data Collection

A Gowerlabs NTS optical tomography system was used to collect the fNIRS data (Everdell et al., 2005). The system had 14 sources and 14 detectors (38 channels) covering the left and right sides of the head over the inferior frontal lobe and temporal lobe (Figure 2). For the two-year-old participants, optodes were inserted into a custom-built headband or an EasyCap. The custom-built headband was used at the beginning of data collection for 15% of the participants and then the EasyCap was used for the remainder of the two-year-old participants. The layout of the optodes was the same for the custom-built and EasyCap headgear, and anatomical localization was performed to account for differences in cap placement (see below for procedure). The EasyCap was used as the headgear for all five-year-old children. The source-detector separation was two cm for all channels on the custom-built headbands. For the EasyCap headgear, the source-detector distance for all channels was 2 cm for cap sizes 48 cm or less, 2.1 cm for the 50 cm cap size, 2.2 cm for the 52 cm cap size, and 2.3 cm for the 54 cm cap size.

### Procedure

Children’s head circumference was measured, and the headgear was placed on the child’s head. Pictures of the front and sides of the head were taken to assess the quality of cap placement. In the optimal cap placement, the cap was placed centrally on top of Cz, the fourth optode from the forehead on the bottom row was located directly above the tragus on each side, and the front of the headgear was placed centrally and straight across the forehead just above the eyebrows. During the experiment, participants listened to the statistical learning paradigm while either sitting on their parents’ lap (at two years old) or on their own on a plastic chair (at five years old) one meter away from a monitor on which the silent cartoon was played. The room was dark, and the paradigm was played at a volume of approximately 74 decibels. The experimenter stood next to the parent and child to calm or redirect the child if needed. The paradigm was paused or terminated as necessary if the child could not be redirected. The session was recorded with a video camera to conduct behavioral coding offline.

### fNIRS Data Preprocessing

The quality of fNIRS data was first assessed using the QT_NIRS toolbox (https://github.com/lpollonini/qt-nirs; Hernandez and Pollonini, 2020). Eight channels were shown to be contaminated by correlation/anticorrelation of the two wavelengths, caused by crosstalk of the encoding frequency of the sources of light paired with the same detector in the fNIRS array (see Figure 2 for position of affected channels). This contamination altered the neurophysiological signal in the eight affected channels and could not be recovered, so they were removed from further analyses for every participant.

Data were then pre-processed in MATLAB version R2020b (The Mathworks, Natick, MA) using the HOMER2 toolbox (Huppert et al., 2009). Channels were excluded if they had very low optical intensity (mean < 0.003 V). Participants were excluded from further analyses if they had more than 12 invalid channels. Raw intensity data were then converted to optical density. Spline interpolation (Scholkmann et al., 2010) and wavelet filtering (Molavi & Dumont, 2012) were both used to correct motion artifacts, because recent work has shown the combination of these two techniques outperforms each individually in developmental datasets (Di Lorenzo et al., 2019). Motion artifacts were identified as signal exceeding a 0.4 change in amplitude in both age groups, and a change in standard deviation of 16 for the two-year-old data and 14 for the five-year-old data within a one-second time window. Data points within one second on either side of the detected motion were marked as motion artifact. Parameters were chosen after visually inspecting a random subset of data for each age group, assessing the performance of the motion detection algorithms, and the impact of different thresholds. Spline interpolation was then applied to these artifact segments. A wavelet motion correction algorithm (IQR = 0.80) was then applied. Motion artifact detection was applied again using the same parameters as above to identify and reject trials with remaining motion artifacts (within −2 to 16 s relative to trial onset).

Behavioral coding was conducted offline using video recordings. Trials were rejected if there was talking, interaction with the child, very loud noises, or crying during the trial or in the preceding baseline period. Participants were excluded if they had less than three valid trials per condition. Participants were also excluded if there was interference for > 40% of the four-minute training phase of the statistical learning paradigm to ensure the child had been adequately exposed to the tone words, following procedures from other statistical learning studies with children (Raviv & Arnon, 2018; Arciuli & Simpson, 2011) and accounting for the common presence of background noise in the study environment. Next, a bandpass filter was applied from 0.03 Hz to 1 Hz. The optical density data were converted to concentration of oxygenated (HbO2) and deoxygenated (HHb) hemoglobin using the modified Beer Lambert Law (partial pathlength filter (ppf)=5 for two-year-olds; ppf=6 for five-year-olds). Data for each participant and each channel were segmented into blocks of 20 seconds of data, including two seconds pre-stimulus onset, a 10 second experimental trial, plus 8 seconds of the following baseline period (used for baseline correction). The time courses of HbO2 and HHb were averaged together for valid trials, for each channel and each participant. The valid trials of each condition were averaged together in each channel at the individual and group level. In the younger-cohort, 210 participants were originally enrolled at six months old, with 102 two-year-olds contributing valid fNIRS data. In the older cohort, 210 participants were enrolled at three-years-old, with 125 five-year-olds contributing valid fNIRS data (Table 1). The most common reason for exclusion was ending the session early in the two-year-olds (N =49) (as children are fussier at this age) and too many bad channels in the five-year-olds (N=48) (as children tend to have thicker and darker hair by this age which contributed to low signal levels).

### Anatomical Localization

Coregistration and anatomical localization was performed on each participant to account for different head sizes and cap placements, following procedures discussed in (Pirazzoli et al., 2022). The two-year-old participants were matched to a close magnetic resonance image (MRI) in the Neurodevelopmental database (Richards et al., 2016; Sanchez et al., 2012) based on age, head circumference, and ear‐to‐ear measurements over the forehead and over the top of the head. A subset of the five-year-old participants had their own MRI scans available (N = 60) and were used for coregistration collected as part of the wider study. The remaining five-year-old participants without their own MRI were matched to a close-matched MRI from another study participant (N = 65), based on age, head circumference, and ear‐to‐ear measurements over the forehead and over the top of the head. A previously developed algorithm was used to place a virtual 3-D array of the fNIRS cap layout onto the MRI head model and ajust to match photographs of the cap placement (Fu & Richards, 2021).

Photon propagation modeling (Fang, 2010) was used to estimate the diffuse optical tomography sensitivity functions from each source and detector pair comprising a channel. The IFG and STG were selected as regions of interest (ROIs) for these analyses (based on LPBA40 atlas). Using diffuse optical tomography data, the sensitivity of each channel to each ROI was estimated for each participant. A channel was assigned to an ROI if its sensitivity to that ROI exceeded a 20% threshold for the two-year-olds and a 15% threshold for the five-year-olds relative to the sensitivity in the whole brain. These thresholds were selected after visual inspection of a subset of participants’ data so that each channel would be largely sensitive to one ROI only. For channels that reached the threshold for both ROIs, that channel was included in the ROI with the higher sensitivity level. ROIs were calculated at the individual level to account for differences in cap placement and head circumference (Figure 3).

### Socioeconomic Status

SES was indexed with two variables, maternal education and adjusted family income. Maternal education was assessed based on mothers’ self-report on a demographics questionnaire administered at enrollment as an oral interview by the local staff. Maternal education was coded as the number of completed years of formal education. Monthly income and number of people in the household were self-reported as part of the demographics questionnaire at enrollment. Family income adjusted for household size was calculated by dividing the monthly family income by the number of household members (henceforth referred to as family income).

### Language Outcomes

Language outcomes were assessed with the Mullen Scales of Early Learning in the younger cohort at two years old and with the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scales of Intelligence, Third Edition (WPPSI-III) in the older cohort at five years old (Wechsler, 1991). Both the Mullen and WPPSI were administered by local psychologists (see Jensen et al., 2019). The Mullen has been used in low-income contexts previously (Bass et al., 2017). The WPPSI has been administered in Bangladesh before and was shown to be locally acceptable (Aboud, 2007). The Mullen and WPPSI were developed and normed for the United States so were adapted to the Bangladeshi context by replacing unfamiliar images and examples with those more familiar with children in Dhaka. Both assessments were translated to Bengali by the study staff. For the two-year-olds, the expressive language and receptive language subscales of the Mullen were standardized and summed to create a composite language score. For the five-year-olds, a Z-score of the verbal intelligence quotient (IQ) from the WPPSI was used as a measure of verbal reasoning.

### Analysis Plan

To address the first aim of this study, the fNIRS data were used to calculate the mean HbO2 and HHb responses within 9–13 seconds post-stimulus onset for the two-year-olds and 10–14 seconds post-stimulus onset for the five-year-olds. The time window of interest for each age group was selected by visually inspecting the group averaged time-courses across channels and selecting a four-second window that included the maximum concentration changes for HbO2 and HHb across most channels (see Figures S1 and S2). To assess whether an earlier time window may have produced different fNIRS results, a repeated measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) was performed with time window (10–14 seconds and 6–10 seconds), ROI, hemisphere, and condition as within-subjects factors and age as a between-subjects factor. Results revealed no main effect of time window, F(1, 86) = 0.11, p = .341, and no significant interactions with time window (p-values > .146). We therefore concluded that our chosen time windows were adequate. Channels included in each ROI (right/left IFG, right/left STG) were averaged together for each of the ROIs in each individual following anatomical localization. T-tests were performed within age for each ROI separately to test whether the HbO2 and HHb mean responses in each ROI were significantly different from baseline (two second pre-stimulus period). False discovery rate (FDR) correction was performed to control for multiple comparisons. Additional t-tests were then performed to test differences in HbO2 mean responses between conditions. Three separate RM-ANOVA tests were then conducted for each condition contrast, with ROI and hemisphere as within-subject factors and age as a between-subject factor.

To address the second aim of this study, associations among SES, fNIRS responses during statistical learning, and language outcomes were assessed. Bivariate Pearson correlations were computed for each variable pairing. The fNIRS variables used in these correlations were the difference in mean HBO2 signal between the High TP and Novel conditions in the left STG and right STG. For cohorts in which a significant association was found between SES measure(s) and language outcomes, an exploratory mediation model was conducted to explore whether the cortical responses during statistical learning measured in this study could represent a potential pathway underlying this association. For the five-year-old cohort, a mediation model was performed using PROCESS version 43 in RStudio (Model 4: Simple mediation) (Hayes, 2022) with bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) to investigate whether neural correlates of statistical learning could partially explain relations between SES and language. The model included maternal education as the predictor, Z-score of verbal IQ at five years as the outcome, and the difference in HbO2 to the High TP and Novel conditions in the right STG as the potential mediator.

### Transparency and Openness

Due to the constraints imposed by the IRB and consent forms used in this study, data cannot be made publicly available on an open-source platform. The data used in this study are available, upon reasonable request, from Dr. Charles A. Nelson (Charles.nelson@childrens.harvard.edu). Code for statistical analyses and sound files of tone words presented in paradigm are publicly available (https://github.com/eilysullivan/fNIRS_statlearning). This study and analysis plan were not preregistered as it was a largely exploratory secondary data analysis conducted after the completion of data collection.

## Results

### Descriptive Statistics

Participants in the two-year-old cohort had an average age of 25.72 months (SD = 2.07 months) and participants in the five-year-old cohort had an average age of 62.35 months (SD = 2.46 months) at the time of fNIRS data collection. Descriptive statistics of measures of SES and language outcomes included in the analyses are displayed in Table 2. The average family income was 30,040.59 Bangladeshi Takas (277.58 USD) per month in the two-year-old cohort and 26,613.18 Takas (245.91 USD) per month in the five-year-old cohort. Sixty percent of the families in the two-year-old cohort and 65% of families in the five-year-old cohort were living in extreme poverty, defined by the World Bank as living on less than the current equivalent of $2.15 per person per day, higher than the average level of impoverishment in the Bangladesh overall (13.5%) (NIPORT & ICF, 2023). The difference in income between the two- and five-year-olds was not significant. Mullen language raw scores and WPPSI verbal IQ scores are reported in Table 2 for descriptive purposes and contextualization, but the sum of Z-scores of the two Mullen language subscales and the Z-score of the WPPSI verbal IQ score are used in all other analyses.

### Aim One: Assessing Statistical learning in Bangladeshi Children with fNIRS

To address the first aim of investigating the feasibility of measuring statistical learning abilities using a tone-based fNIRS task in Bangladeshi children, we examined changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin levels in response to the three conditions of varying predictability. The time-courses of oxygenated, deoxygenated, and total hemoglobin for each condition in the four ROIs are displayed in Figure 4. (Channel-level time-courses are displayed in Figures S1 and S2). T-tests were performed in each ROI, separately for each age group, to assess whether the oxygenated hemoglobin responses to the statistical learning conditions were significantly different from baseline (silence) (Table S1 and Figure S3). Within each condition and age group, FDR correction was performed to assess whether effects would remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. At two years old, HbO2 responses to High TP and Low TP conditions, but not the Novel condition, were significantly different from baseline in the left and right STG (p-values < .005), and all tests survived FDR correction. The left and right IFG were not significantly activated in any of the conditions in the two-year-old cohort. At five years old, HbO2 responses were significantly different from baseline in the left and right STG to all conditions (p-values < .026), although activation in the left STG to the High TP condition did not survive FDR correction. The responses to conditions in the left and right IFG were not significantly different from baseline, except for the response to the Low TP condition in the left IFG (p = .027) (which did not survive FDR correction). These results suggest that fNIRS can be utilized to show evidence of statistical learning in both two- and five-year-olds in this context, and the STG may be more involved in statistical learning processes than the IFG.

Following examination of the fNIRS responses during statistical learning compared to baseline, we next examined whether the fNIRS responses to the conditions were different from one another (High TP versus Novel, High TP versus Low TP, Low TP versus Novel) to understand whether children’s brain responses differed based on the predictability of the auditory sequences. T-tests were employed to assess the statistical significance of these condition contrasts for both HbO2 and HHb responses. Results of the t-tests are displayed in Table 3 and Figure 5.

We first tested the contrast in hemodynamic responses between the High TP and Novel conditions to assess differences in fNIRS responses to very predictable versus unpredictable auditory patterns. The two-year-old cohort showed significant discrimination between the High TP and Novel conditions in the right STG (t(101) = 2.934, p = .004), with a higher HbO2 response to the High TP condition than the Novel condition. There was no significant difference in responses to the High TP versus Novel condition in the other ROIs for the two-year-olds. The five-year-old cohort also showed significant differentiation between the High TP and Novel conditions in the right STG (t(119) = −5.120, p < .001), as well as in the left STG (t(119) = −2.124, p < .036) (although this contrast did not survive FDR correction). Of note, the discrimination was in the opposite direction as the two-year-old cohort. The five-year-old cohort displayed a higher HbO2 response to the Novel condition than the High TP condition, whereas the two-year-old cohort showed the opposite with a higher response to the High TP than the Novel condition. The five-year-old cohort did not show significant differentiation between the High TP and Novel conditions in the left or right IFG. Overall, these results suggest that when comparing fNIRS responses to very familiar versus unpredictable auditory patterns, two-year-olds exhibit higher brain activity during the familiar patterns in the right STG, whereas five-year-olds exhibited the opposite pattern with higher brain activity following the unpredictable patterns.

We next tested whether fNIRS responses differed between very predictable (High TP) and somewhat predictable (Low TP) auditory patterns. Both the two- and five-year-old cohort showed no significant differentiation between these two conditions in any ROI, suggesting that this contrast in predictability was too subtle for either age group to detect.

We then tested the remaining condition contrast by assessing whether fNIRS responses differed between somewhat familiar (Low TP) and unpredictable (Novel) auditory patterns. The two-year-old cohort did not show significant differentiation in any ROI, indicating that brain responses were comparable somewhat predictable and novel auditory patterns. The five-year-old cohort showed higher HbO2 responses to the Novel condition than the Low TP condition in the right STG (t(119) = −6.018 p < .002) and left STG (t(119) = −2.022, p < .045) (although the contrast in the left STG did not survive FDR correction). These findings suggest that five-year-olds may be able to detect smaller differences in probabilities than two-year-olds, as their brain responses were significantly higher for the Novel patterns than the somewhat predictable (Low TP) patterns, while the two-year-olds did not show this differentiation.

We next conducted RM-ANOVAs for each HbO2 condition contrast separately to further examine the differences between conditions and assess possible effects of age, ROI, and hemisphere. For the difference between the very familiar (High TP) and Novel fNIRS HbO2 responses, the RM-ANOVA revealed significant main effects of age, F(1, 195) = 9.051, p = .003 and hemisphere, F(1, 195) = 5.072, p =.025. Post-hoc t-testing revealed that the difference between the conditions in the two-year-old cohort (M = 0.034) was significantly higher than in the five-year-old cohort (M = −0.019) (p = .003). These findings provide further evidence for higher activation to familiar tone sequences for the two-year-olds (indicated by a positive average value for this High TP – Novel contrast) and higher activation to novel tone sequences in the two-year-olds (indicated by a positive average value for this High TP – Novel contrasts). The difference between the two conditions was significantly greater in the left hemisphere (M = 0.018) than in the right hemisphere (M = −0.004) (p = .025), indicating more differentiation in brain responses in the left hemisphere to auditory patterns with different predictability levels than in the right hemisphere. There was a significant interaction between age and ROI, F(1, 195) = 12.954, p < .001. Post-hoc testing revealed that this interaction may have been driven by the right STG, which showed a significant difference between the two-year-old and five-year-old cohorts for the High TP versus Novel condition, (t(219.96) = −2.185, p = .030), although this test did not survive FDR correction. The High TP versus Novel contrast was not significantly different in the left STG, left IFG, or right IFG (p-values > .110).

The RM-ANOVA for the High TP versus Low TP contrast revealed no main effects of ROI, age, or hemisphere, suggesting that fNIRS responses to very predictable and somewhat predictable auditory patterns were similar across the cohorts and brain regions.

The RM-ANOVA for the somewhat predictable (Low TP) versus Novel contrast revealed no main effect of ROI or hemisphere, indicating similar brain responses to these different types of auditory patterns across the brain regions investigated. There was a significant difference in age cohorts for the contrast in HbO2 responses between the Low TP and Novel conditions, F(1, 195) = 5.849, p = .017. The difference between the Low TP and Novel conditions was higher (more positive) in the two-year-old cohort (M = 0.017) than in the five-year-old cohort (M = −0.028). The five-year-old cohort showed a negative difference value between the two conditions (whereas the two-year-old cohort showed a positive difference value), but a greater absolute magnitude of difference than the two-year-old cohort, possibly indicating greater ability to discriminate subtle contrasts in probabilities of auditory patterns. There was also a significant interaction between ROI and age cohort, F(1, 195) = 4.650, p = .032. The left and right hemispheres were averaged together and post-hoc t-testing was performed to explore this interaction, revealing that there was no significant difference between the cohorts in either the left/right IFG (p = .375) or the left/right STG (p = .451), indicating that this interaction was not driven by one particular ROI.

### Aim Two: Exploring Relations among SES, fNIRS, and Language

To address our second aim of exploring whether fNIRS responses during this statistical learning task are sensitive to individual differences in SES or language outcomes, the selected measures of SES (maternal education and adjusted family income) and language outcomes (Mullen language composite Z-score for two-year-olds and WPPSI verbal IQ Z-score for five-year-olds) were examined in relation to selected fNIRS measures (the magnitude of the HbO2 contrast between the High TP and Novel contrast in the left and right STG), as these measures were of the most theoretical interest and showed significant differentiation between the High TP and Novel in the left and/or right STG in the two- and five-year-old cohorts).

Bivariate Pearson correlations were computed to examine associations between pairs of variables (Figure 6). Scatterplots of these relations can be found in Figure S4. In the two-year-olds, significant associations were found between the two indices of SES, as higher family income was significantly associated with higher maternal education (p < .001). At two years old, there were no significant associations between SES measures and language outcomes. Additionally, fNIRS measures of interest were not significantly related to SES or fNIRS measures of interest.

In the five-year-olds, higher family income was related to higher maternal education (p < .001). Higher maternal education levels were found to be associated with higher WPPSI language scores in this cohort (p < .001). Both measures of SES were significantly negatively correlated with the difference in HbO2 responses to the High TP and Novel conditions in the right STG (p-values < .05); family income was also significantly negatively associated with the High TP versus Novel HbO2 responses in the left STG (p-values < .05). Given there was an overall negative difference between High TP and Novel conditions (with higher response to the Novel condition), these negative correlations indicate that higher SES is associated with increased differentiation between predictable and unpredictable tone sequences in the STG. Neither fNIRS measure of interest was correlated with the WPPSI language outcome at five years old.

Because no significant associations between SES, neural correlates of statistical learning, and language outcomes were found in the two-year-old cohort, no further analyses were conducted. In the five-year-old cohort, given significant associations found between variables of interest, an exploratory mediation model was conducted to assess whether the relation between maternal education and WPPSI scores were partially explained by the difference in the contrast in oxygenated hemoglobin fNIRS responses to the High TP and Novel conditions in the right STG. The results from Model 4 (simple mediation) using PROCESS version 43 in RStudio (Hayes, 2022) with 5,000 resamples revealed that the indirect effect of maternal education on WPPSI language outcomes through the difference in fNIRS oxygenated hemoglobin levels to the High TP and Novel conditions in the right STG was not significant (B = 0.002, Bootstrapped SE = 0.004, Bootstrapped 95% CI [−0.005, 0.013]). Thus, while higher SES (as indexed by maternal education) was related to higher language outcomes in the five-year-old cohort, it appears that this association does not operate through the selected neural correlates during the statistical learning task and alternative potential mediators should be explored.

## Discussion

The goals of the current study were to (1) investigate the feasibility of utilizing fNIRS to measure brain responses during a tone-based statistical learning task in Bangladeshi children, and (2) to explore whether these fNIRS correlates could be sensitive to individual differences in SES and language. To our knowledge, this is the first study to use fNIRS to investigate auditory statistical learning in these age groups in an LMIC. Addressing our first aim, we found evidence of statistical learning abilities in both the two- and five-year-old cohort, demonstrating the feasibility of utilizing a tone-based paradigm with fNIRS to index statistical learning abilities in an LMIC and in these age groups. We found that the STG, but not the IFG was implicated in statistical learning in both the two- and five-year-old cohort during the current paradigm. These findings provide further support for the STG playing a role in auditory processing and discrimination in statistical learning (Emberson et al., 2015; Tremblay et al., 2013; Arimitsu et al., 2011). Yet, these findings contradict other statistical learning studies which have implicated frontal areas (Karuza et al., 2013; Abla & Okanoya, 2008), possibly because prior work often used linguistic stimuli such as syllables in their statistical learning paradigms, whereas we used non-linguistic tones (Arimitsu et al., 2011; Petersson et al., 2004). Thus, the STG may play a more important role than the IFG in processing the current statistical learning paradigm.

Notably, the five-year-olds showed significant discrimination in the right STG for both the High TP versus Novel and Low TP versus Novel contrasts, whereas the two-year-olds showed significant discrimination in the right STG for only the High TP vs. Novel contrast. Together, these findings may suggest that this tone-based statistical learning task can index age differences in statistical learning abilities, as five-year-olds appear to be more advanced in their statistical learning capacities, given their ability to discriminate smaller differences in probability than the two-year-olds.

Interestingly, the two-year-olds exhibited significantly higher responses to the High TP condition than the Novel condition in the right STG, whereas the five-year-olds exhibited the opposite pattern. This was somewhat unexpected because, as detailed in the introduction, higher activation during novelty sequences is often seen in infants and higher activation during familiar sequences are often seen in adults during statistical learning (Abla & Okanoya, 2008; Hasson & Tremblay 2016; Emberson et al., 2015). Few studies of responses to novel versus familiar sequences during tone-based statistical learning have been conducted in early childhood, and thus further investigation is needed to confirm whether there could be multiple shifts in responses between infancy and adulthood, and whether these patterns of findings would be consistent with other cultures or contexts at these ages.

To address our second aim of exploring whether fNIRS correlates from this statistical learning paradigm could serve as indices of individual variation in SES and language abilities, we explored relations among the environmental, neuroimaging, and outcome data. At two years old, we found no associations between SES and our fNIRS measures of interest. At five years old, we did find that higher SES measures were related to a larger difference between fNIRS responses to the novel and familiar tone sequences in the STG, or a larger (more negative) difference in oxy-Hb response between the Novel and High TP conditions. These results suggest that higher SES may be related to larger differentiation in brain responses to tone patterns of differing levels of predictability by age five, demonstrating that this statistical learning paradigm may be sensitive to individual differences in environmental circumstances and could provide an index of the biological embedding of SES. Additionally, SES was found to be related to language outcomes at five years, but not at two years. These observations are consistent with other findings from the BEAN project which have revealed more associations between adversity and neuroimaging measures at older ages than at younger ages in infancy and childhood (Jensen et al., 2021; Pirazzoli et al., 2022), as well as behavioral studies in other LMICs which show that SES-based gaps in child development outcomes tend to emerge across the early childhood period (e.g., Fernald et al., 2012). Thus, it is plausible that no associations were found in the two-year-old cohort because early adversity may take time to show measurable impacts on certain brain measures (Jensen et al., 2021). The first two years of life could serve as a window for effective early intervention before some experiences show effects on brain development. Overall, while we cannot establish causal pathways by which SES is related to statistical learning, this work represents a first step towards establishing the feasibility of utilizing fNIRS measures to investigate SES-related variation in statistical learning in an LMIC and can foster future work to interrogate the mechanisms underlying these associations.

We found that the fNIRS measures of interest were not associated with language outcomes at two or five years of age. This was not consistent with our hypothesis, as previous literature has documented associations between statistical learning and language abilities (Kidd & Arciuli, 2016; Evans, 2009). Additionally, statistical learning fNIRS correlates were not found to mediate associations found between SES and language abilities at five years. It is possible that we may have found links with language outcomes if we used linguistic stimuli such as syllables or words that are more directly related to the language outcome measures than tones. Additionally, at two and five years, there may be more influential factors than statistical learning contributing to language outcomes (e.g., language exposure, vocabulary, phonological processing) (Demir & Küntay, 2014). Furthermore, the language measures used in this study, the Mullen and WPPSI, were originally developed for Western contexts. While the tests were adapted to the local context, it is possible that these measures are still not well suited to accurately assessing language abilities in this setting. The lack of significant findings is important to note as they demonstrate that while this paradigm may be well-suited to indexing individual differences in SES by five years of age, alternative paradigms should be used if a researcher’s goal is to examine links between statistical learning and individual differences in language abilities.

Overall, in this study we demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing fNIRS during a tone-based paradigm to detect statistical learning responses in two- and five-year-olds in an LMIC context. However, there are a few limitations to this study that should be considered. First, we only had access to Bangladeshi MRIs for the anatomical localization of the five-year-old fNIRS data and thus we used U.S. MRIs for the two-year-old data. Differences in fNIRS findings between the two- and five-year-old cohort could be due to the difference in coregistration methods, although careful matching procedures at the individual level were performed to limit effects of head-shape and head-size differences between U.S. and Bangladeshi MRIs. We also were unable to include eight channels in our analyses due to technical crosstalk issues, and thus the ROIs may have been more distributed with the inclusion of these channels. Also, we were unable to examine the impact of our inclusion of “late-preterm” children (born 34 to 36 weeks of age) in the sample, which could be a confounding factor given recent evidence on the developmental trajectories of “late-preterm” infants (Stewart et al., 2019). It is also important to note that there may be important protective factors or socialization practices that influence language development in this context that we were unable to assess in the current analyses. To expand on the current study, in the future we aim to investigate potential protective factors, combine the current sample with additional higher-income cohorts from the BEAN study to explore wider socioeconomic variability, and follow up with the children at older ages to assess relations with school performance. Importantly, this study’s investigation of statistical learning was largely exploratory to establish feasibility of these tools in an LMIC. We do not have the ability to disentangle exactly how SES relates to fNIRS correlates of statistical learning. Future studies should involve experiments with manipulation of the current paradigm to investigate whether more general auditory processing, attention to stimuli, ability to detect rapid fleeting information, or discrimination of the predictability of auditory patterns are driving relations with early experiences. Intervention studies are also needed to establish whether relations between SES and fNIRS responses during this paradigm are causal.

This study establishes the feasibility of utilizing fNIRS to index statistical learning responses in an LMIC population of two- and five-year-olds. This is the first study to our knowledge to utilize a statistical learning fNIRS paradigm in an LMIC in these age groups. We found differences between the age groups in discrimination of probabilities, responses to familiar vs. novel sequences, and associations with SES, suggesting the need for further investigation into the age-related changes in statistical learning during childhood. Establishing the feasibility of utilizing this tone-based statistical learning paradigm can open the door to administering the same paradigm in diverse settings to understand the extent to which the development of brain responses during statistical learning are universal or vary across contexts and cultures. The associations found between SES and fNIRS measures at five years old suggest that a tone-based statistical learning paradigm may be a useful tool to examine how individual variation in environmental circumstances is biologically embedded. Further investigation is needed to expand on this exploratory study to elucidate the causal mechanisms underlying associations between SES and the neural correlates of statistical learning in LMICs.
